courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: Tagged pointers: a version counter beside the pointer
md: Tagged pointer = pointer plus a counter compared and swapped as one unit, bumped on every successful CAS. It turns "same value" into "same value and same version".

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Per-query deltas, paired tests and confidence intervals
md: Queries are not the only noise source. If a stage is trained, its score also varies with the random seed. Use the same seeds and checkpoints for every stage you are not ablating, and when the ablated stage itself is retrained, run several seeds and report the spread, or a seed-to-seed swing can masquerade as a component effect.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Sequential vs random ids, and why random ids are not authorization
md: Parler's public posts were meant to be readable one at a time. Sequential ids plus no rate limit turned "anyone can read a post" into "anyone can copy the entire site, with GPS locations". Authorization decides who may read an object; rate limits and unpredictable ids decide how cheaply someone can read all of them. You need both.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: What Active Directory is: one directory for thousands of machines
md: A domain is not a wall. Domains in one forest trust each other automatically, and the Enterprise Admins group of the forest root is an administrator in every domain (next lesson). Plan protection for the whole forest, not one domain at a time.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: AS-REP roasting and password spraying against AD
md: Turning off pre-authentication hands out crackable material to anyone; 4768 with pre-auth type 0 finds it. Spraying hides under per-account lockout; count distinct accounts per source in 4771 and 4776, not failures per account.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Tiered administration, Protected Users and LAPS
md: Tiering fails quietly through agents. A backup, monitoring or patching tool that runs as SYSTEM on DCs, managed from a Tier 1 console, makes that console Tier 0. List everything installed on DCs and everyone who controls it.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: PDF: objects, filters, automatic actions and JavaScript
md: Do not open a suspicious PDF in your everyday reader to 'see what it says'. Readers run JavaScript and follow actions; that is the point of the file. Triage with pdfid and parse with pdf-parser, which only read bytes.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Ransomware crypto mistakes: how Hive's files were decrypted
md: Crypto flaws in ransomware are rare, and once published they can be fixed in the next version. Plan recovery around offline backups; treat a decryptor as a lucky bonus, and get one only from a trusted source.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: What this means for engineers: safe languages, fuzzing, defaults
md: Prevent, then detect, then mitigate. Memory-safe languages remove bug classes; sanitizers and fuzzing catch what remains; mitigations on by default raise the cost of what slips through; and fast patching shortens the window. Every rung an attacker must climb is one you can remove.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Scoring outcomes and measuring detection coverage
md: Averages hide shapes. An average score of 3 can be every technique alerting but never triaged, or half the techniques perfect and half invisible. Always report the distribution and the gap categories with the average, and never report coverage as "techniques with a rule tagged".

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: tau-bench: simulated users, database state and pass^k
md: The paper calls r = 1 necessary but not sufficient: an agent that issues the correct return *without* asking for confirmation still scores 1, even though it broke policy. Database comparison catches wrong outcomes, not bad conduct along the way.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Permissions, traces and evaluation
md: Permission checks are only as strong as the sandbox behind them. Anthropic recommends extensive testing in sandboxed environments for agents; run untrusted or autonomous agents in a container or VM with limited network and credentials, and reserve modes that skip approval for those isolated environments.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Why an agent saying done is not evidence of done
md: Misconception: if the agent ran the tests itself and reported success, the work is verified. The report is model output, and tests the agent wrote or could edit are not independent. Run the checks in the harness, on a clean copy, with tests the agent did not control.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: How an LLM app is built: one stream of tokens
md: An LLM app has one channel. Instructions and data are both tokens in the context window, and the model, not your code, decides what each token means.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Approval gates and egress allowlists
md: Gate side effects with a real, informed human decision. Constrain network egress to exact hosts in code the model cannot influence. Together they turn "the model was fooled" into "the model asked and was refused".

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Defence in layers: privilege separation, provenance and egress
md: Design so that a fully hijacked model still cannot do harm: it cannot reach what it should not read, cannot act without a check it cannot talk past, and cannot send data anywhere you did not list.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Why AI text needs a planted signal
md: A text watermark is a keyed, pseudorandom preference applied at sampling time. Detection re-derives the preference from the text and asks whether the text agrees with it far more often than chance.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Attacks on text watermarks: edits, paraphrase, spoofing and stealing
md: Text watermarks fail in four ways: edits that re-randomize the seeds, meaning-preserving rewrites, spoofing that plants the signal in text the provider never wrote, and stealing by learning the pattern. Treat a positive detection as statistical evidence about origin, not proof of authorship, and a negative one as no information.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Why the mean and standard deviation hide outliers
md: A score is only as good as its model of normal. Mean and standard deviation break under masking; median and MAD fix that for one variable. For data with clusters and local structure you need scores that look at the joint shape of the data, which is what the next lessons build.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Evaluating detectors when 1 percent of points are anomalies
md: Under heavy imbalance, judge detectors by ranking quality where you will act: AP and the PR curve for the whole ranking, precision@k for the review budget. ROC-AUC hides false alarms because it divides them by the huge number of normal points.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: The authorization code flow with PKCE, step by step
md: The code travels through the browser, so assume it can leak. PKCE ties redeeming it to a secret that never left the client that started the flow.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Classic JWT bugs: alg none, RS256 to HS256, kid and jku
md: Every one of these bugs is the same mistake: letting data inside the unverified token decide how the token is verified. The receiver fixes the algorithm, the key set and the audience; the token only gets to say which of the receiver's keys it used.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Design review in the cycle: deciding which changes get a threat model
md: A design review that happens after the code is written is an audit, not a design review. If the triage questionnaire lives in the pull request template instead of the design template, the expensive decisions (which vendor, where the data lives) are already made.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Security champions, bug bounties and disclosure programmes
md: Champions scale security inside; a VDP with safe harbour invites help from outside. Both fail without the basics: someone answers the reports, and fixes have owners and deadlines.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Why a crash needs both undo and redo
md: Steal creates the need for **undo**, no-force creates the need for **redo**. ARIES allows both, so it must do both, using only the log and a little state stored on each page.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Four ways to tell the model which side a text is on
md: All four designs encode the same idea: one shared vector space, two roles. Use the exact pair (prefixes, instructions or input types) that the model was trained with, on the side it was trained for.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Batch jobs, idempotent pipelines and putting it together
md: Order of checks for each call: cache first (free, instant), then dedupe in-flight duplicates, then a concurrency limit and a rate limiter, then the API with bounded jittered retries. Anything that is not latency-sensitive goes to a batch job. Every side effect is keyed so that re-running the job is safe.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Compare-and-swap: write only if nothing changed, else retry
md: CAS turns "read, compute, write" into "read, compute, write *only if what I read is still there*". The retry loop is the general recipe: load, compute from the loaded value, CAS, and on failure recompute from the value CAS returned.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Zero-shot classification with CLAP audio and text embeddings
md: Choosing an approach: use a pretrained tagger's scores directly when AudioSet classes cover your needs; train a small head on frozen embeddings when you have a few hundred labeled clips; fine-tune when you have more data and compute; use CLAP-style zero-shot when labels change often or you have no labeled audio, and expect lower accuracy than a supervised head on the same classes.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Online attacks: brute force, credential stuffing, password spraying
md: Brute force is one account, many passwords. Credential stuffing is many leaked pairs. Spraying is one password, many accounts. MFA and breached-password checks defeat all three; detection needs counts across accounts, not just per account.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Why research needs a loop, not one retrieval
md: A research agent is not a bigger retrieval call. It is a harness loop whose next query depends on what the last read revealed, and whose output is a set of claims each tied to a source.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: On-demand capacity: tokens per minute and the max_tokens trap
md: Set `max_tokens` close to the longest answer you really need. The AWS docs say it directly: if you hit TPM quotas earlier than expected, reduce max_tokens to better approximate your completions. Measure real output lengths from the `OutputTokenCount` metric that Bedrock publishes to CloudWatch, the AWS monitoring service.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Firmware images: layout, signatures and entropy
md: Everything here uses an image we built from our own code. Real vendor firmware is often covered by licence terms, and some contains other parties' secrets; analyse only devices and images you own or are authorised to test, and never download firmware to attack devices you do not control.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Does ternary scale? The evidence and its limits
md: Read the scale. The accuracy evidence in the b1.58 paper stops at 3.9B parameters and 100B tokens, plus one 3B model at 2T tokens. Everything larger is a measurement of speed, memory and energy, not of quality.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Counters and history: how a predictor learns a pattern
md: Predictors learn *regularity*: biased branches, periodic patterns, and (next lesson) correlations with other branches. A branch on random data with a 50/50 split is mispredicted about half the time on every CPU, no matter how clever the predictor.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: IPC and Mojo: the renderer asks, the browser decides
md: Ask of every IPC method: which argument identifies *who is asking*, and does the privileged side get that from its own state or from the message? Identity must come from the browser's state. Everything in the message is attacker input to be range-checked, type-checked and allowlisted.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: Who finds browser bugs: bounties, in-the-wild 0-days and practice
md: Across every case in this course the pattern is the same: one bug class (type confusion, use-after-free, a stale check, a trusted value from a less privileged process), one boundary it crossed, and one fix that either corrects the logic or moves the boundary. Defenders win the n-day race by knowing which of their products sit behind which boundary.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Choosing an engine: tradeoffs, write stalls and failure modes
md: No engine minimizes read, write and space amplification at once. B+trees pay on random writes. Leveled LSMs pay in rewrites. Tiered LSMs pay in reads and temporary space. Pick the cost your workload can afford, then tune T, Bloom bits and compaction bandwidth.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Business impact analysis: from processes to tolerable downtime
md: Do not let IT set the MTD by asking "how fast could we restore it?". That gives you the current capability, not the requirement. The BIA asks the process owner "how long until this becomes unacceptable?", and the gap between the two answers is the work of the rest of this course.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Restoring at the right size: Atlassian's two-week outage, April 2022
md: Granularity is a recovery requirement. In multi-tenant systems (one data store, many customers), "restore the database" also rolls back every unaffected customer. Write RTOs per restore size (one record, one tenant, many tenants, everything) and test each, because they are different procedures with very different times.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Crisis management: decisions, workarounds and communication
md: Do not let the recovery team be the crisis team. Engineers in the middle of a restore should not also be negotiating with customers and drafting press statements; and executives should not be choosing which database snapshot to restore. Separate the roles, connect them with a fixed reporting rhythm.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Build it: a byte GPT, then a two-level patch model
md: A byte GPT is a GPT with a 256-entry vocabulary; the cost is more positions per byte. A two-level model fixes that by running the big network once per patch, and stays causal only through two shifts: one patch for the global input, one byte for the local input.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Why C memory bugs compile cleanly and ship
md: Tools such as AddressSanitizer and **fuzzing** (feeding the program huge numbers of automatically generated or mutated inputs and watching for crashes) find many of these bugs, but only on inputs that actually run. The Android team describes them as treating symptoms rather than the root cause, and notes that coverage stays low without constant pressure on teams to fuzz and triage.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Build a safe type on unsafe: a minimal Vec from scratch
md: Recipe for an unsafe-backed type: write the invariants down, keep the fields they mention private, make every unsafe block's SAFETY comment cite one invariant, and run tests that hit the edges (empty, first grow, full, drop with live elements) under Miri.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Where a line may live: sets, ways and tags
md: Capacity is set by size, conflicts by associativity and address bits. A bigger cache fixes capacity misses; more ways or a less regular stride fixes conflict misses; nothing but prefetching (loading lines before the program asks for them, lesson 4) hides cold misses.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Pruning by influence and grouping supernodes
md: Influence is unsigned. A feature that strongly *inhibits* the answer scores as high as one that promotes it. Use influence to decide what to look at, then read the signed edges to decide what it does.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Inverse propensity scoring turns clicks into unbiased labels
md: Only clicked documents need propensities, and the estimate is unbiased only if the propensities are correct and every relevant document has a nonzero chance of being observed. Joachims et al. also require that propensities depend only on logged information (unconfoundedness).

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Framework auto-escaping and its escape hatches
md: "It comes from our own API" is not the same as "trusted". The value was typed by some user before your API stored it. React's own Markdown example is safe only because the rendered HTML is shown back to the same user who wrote it, and because the team trusts the Markdown parser to have no bugs.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Temperature: why CLIP multiplies cosines by up to 100
md: The temperature turns a ranking of small cosine gaps into a confident probability. Its value decides how sharply the loss concentrates on hard negatives, which is why CLIP learns it and caps the logit scale at 100 for stability.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Your own rules: key abuse, persistence and log tampering
md: Misconception: "ATT&CK IDs are permanent". MITRE reorganises the matrix: Disable or Modify Cloud Log moved from T1562.008 to T1685.002, and tactics have been renamed. Map rules to IDs, but review the mapping when a new ATT&CK version ships.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Code Spaces 2014: why one account is one blast radius
md: Design as if any one credential will be stolen tomorrow. The test of an architecture is not "can an attacker get in?" but "what can one stolen login destroy or read?" Keep the data and its last good copy behind different identities, in different accounts.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Azure in depth: role assignments, Run Command and PIM
md: In Azure, the keys to escalation are writing role assignments and running code where a privileged identity lives. Make powerful roles eligible through PIM, delegate assignments with conditions instead of Owner, and treat Virtual Machine Contributor on a VM as equal to that VM's managed identity.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Long-lived keys vs temporary credentials: STS and Uber 2016
md: Prefer roles and temporary credentials everywhere. AWS's own best practices say to require human users to use federation with temporary credentials and to require workloads to use IAM roles. Long-term access keys are for the few cases nothing else supports, and they need rotation, monitoring and the narrowest possible permissions.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: What k-means actually optimises
md: Scaling is a modelling choice, not a cleanup step. Standardising says "one standard deviation of every feature counts the same", which silently gives a noisy, unimportant feature as much say as a crucial one. Decide how much each feature should weigh, then scale to match. k-means, DBSCAN's eps and every method in this course measure distance, and none of them is scale free.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Evaluating a clustering with and without labels
md: Look at the first two bars. The k = 2 clustering with the *better* inertia, 28.8333, scores ARI 0.4109, while the local optimum with the worse inertia, 30.4167, scores 0.7734. Optimising the objective harder moved the answer away from the truth. Inertia is a proxy, and this is what it means for a proxy to be imperfect: never argue from inertia to correctness.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: SIMD, compiled queries and where columnar engines hit limits
md: Columnar storage cuts bytes moved; vectorized execution cuts instructions per byte. SIMD multiplies the second only when data is dense and in cache.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Why code breaks at -O2: undefined behavior as an optimization license
md: The optimizer assumes the program has no UB: signed overflow never happens, differently typed pointers never alias, dereferenced pointers are not null. Code that breaks those rules can change behavior at -O2. Find it with sanitizers and the -fwrapv, -fno-strict-aliasing and -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks switches, then fix the code.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: The observe-act loop: screenshots in, mouse and keyboard out
md: A computer-use agent is an ordinary agent loop where the tool is "the computer" and the observation is a screenshot. The model proposes actions in screenshot pixel coordinates; the harness executes them, and is the only place you can enforce scaling, safety and verification.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: How loom takes over the scheduler and walks every schedule
md: loom only sees what goes through loom types. A `std::sync::Mutex` or a third-party lock inside your code still runs, but loom cannot schedule around it, so executions that are possible in reality are silently not modeled. Libraries you depend on need loom support too for full coverage.

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: iCT, sCM, LCM and the other few-step distillers
md: Consistency models learn the end of the ODE trajectory, not its slope. The boundary condition anchors the chain at the data; adjacent-time agreement (from a teacher's ODE step or from the data itself) propagates it to high noise; extra steps re-noise and jump again to trade compute for quality.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: The hash ring: each key goes to the next node clockwise
md: Consistent hashing minimises *movement*. It does not by itself give *balance*. With one random token per node, arcs vary wildly in size, as the toy ring shows. The next lesson fixes that.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Why scheduling explodes, and what a constraint model is
md: A constraint solver separates **what** a solution is (the model) from **how** to find it (the search). You declare variables, domains and constraints; the solver chooses the order of guesses and the deductions. Adding a rule means adding one constraint, not rewriting a search loop.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: One kernel, many tenants: the container threat model
md: A container is a fenced process on a shared kernel. Threat-model it as "attacker has a shell in this process" and ask which credentials, network paths and kernel interfaces that shell can touch.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: The API server is the front door: authn, authz, admission
md: Every request passes authentication (401 if unknown), authorization (403 if not allowed), then admission (mutate, then validate) before etcd. Reads skip admission, so RBAC alone protects them. Turn on audit logging, because it is off unless you configure it.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Network policies: from default allow to default deny
md: Pods are non-isolated until a policy selects them. Start each namespace with default deny for both directions, add DNS, then add one allow per intended connection, on both sides.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a hardening map and where to practise
md: No single control holds. Minimal signed images, Restricted pods, least-privilege RBAC, default-deny networks, encrypted and narrowly readable Secrets, authenticated node APIs, patched runtimes, and two kinds of detection: each covers what the others miss.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Resolving the second one and those against what was shown
md: Do not ask the LLM to copy job ids out of text. Give it the shown list with positions and attributes and let it output a position or an attribute match; code does the lookup. A model that types ids can produce a well-formed id that was never shown.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Hidden computation: filler tokens, encoded reasoning, paraphrasing
md: Misconception: "filler tokens did not help, so all of a model's reasoning must be in the words." Lanham's result shows that particular models did not learn to use filler. Pfau et al. show training can teach a transformer to compute across meaningless tokens on suitable problems, and nothing in a monitor's view of "......" would reveal what was computed.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Why CoT is monitorable at all, and how to keep it so
md: These methods sit uneasily with "keep optimization pressure off the CoT". VFT trains directly on CoT content. The difference from Baker et al.'s failure is direction and timing: it rewards saying more, before RL, and the RL reward never reads the CoT. VFT was tested on one 8B model with multiple-choice cues; whether it holds for frontier agents is open.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Packing the pair: special tokens, segments and the 512-token limit
md: A larger max_length is not free and not always possible. Position embeddings fix the hard limit at training time (512 for BERT), and compute per pair grows with sequence length. For long documents, chunk and take the max (or another aggregate) instead of hoping truncation keeps the right part.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Encoding, hashing and encryption are three different things
md: A hash of a short or guessable value is not secret. There are only 10,000 four-digit PINs; hashing all of them takes a fraction of a second, so a stored SHA-256 of a PIN is as good as the PIN. Lesson 11 covers how passwords must be stored instead.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: RSA with tiny numbers: encryption, signing and padding
md: If you ever write pow(m, e, n) in production code you have built textbook RSA. Call a library's OAEP or PSS function, or better, avoid RSA encryption entirely and use an elliptic-curve key exchange plus an AEAD.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Signature nonces: reuse, weak randomness and deterministic signing
md: Two identical signatures of the same message are harmless with RFC 6979. The alarm is the same r value on two different messages under one key: that means k repeated, and the private key must be considered public.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Why a fast GEMM is a hierarchy of tiles
md: Intensity per tile is not the whole story. Two CTAs that share a row of tiles both read the same slice of A, and the L2 cache may serve the second read. CUTLASS's threadblock rasterization (swizzling the CTA launch order: remapping launch indices to tile coordinates so that CTAs running at the same time cover a compact patch of tiles rather than one long row) exists to make that L2 reuse more likely.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: The CUTLASS 3.x API, epilogues and tuning tradeoffs
md: A tile that maximizes arithmetic intensity can still lose: it may leave a tail wave, spill registers, or leave too little shared memory for stages. Measure with the CUTLASS profiler across candidate configurations rather than trusting one formula.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Three questions before you touch a system: law, permission, ethics
md: "It was public, so it was allowed" is the most common mistake. The ACM Code of Ethics says it directly: "A system being publicly accessible is not sufficient grounds on its own to imply authorization." Lesson 4 shows the opposite mistake too: officials calling ordinary viewing of a public page a crime.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: The UK Computer Misuse Act, section by section
md: CMA: s1 knowingly unauthorised access attempt (2 years); s2 with intent to commit a further offence (5); s3 unauthorised impairment (10); s3ZA serious damage (14 or life); s3A tools for those offences (2). Authorisation must come from someone entitled to control that kind of access.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Export controls: Wassenaar and 'intrusion software'
md: Wassenaar (2013, amended 2017) controls intrusion software platforms and development technology, with carve-outs for vulnerability disclosure and incident response. The US implements it through BIS's 2021 rule and License Exception ACE; destination, end user and intended unauthorised use decide when a licence is needed.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Cover-ups and whistleblowing: Uber's CSO and Twitter's security lead
md: When the problem is your own organisation: record the facts, escalate internally to the top, take legal advice, and use lawful external channels (regulators, law enforcement) if ignored. Never relabel a breach, pay for silence, or mislead an investigator.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Fitting a mixing law: RegMix, data mixing laws, judging a mixture
md: Regression methods learn mixture to loss from many cheap runs and search the fit. They work when the fitted function has the right shape and accurate parameters: a linear fit picks a corner, and mis-set laws can lose to uniform weights. Always compare against stratified sampling, and judge data choices with small models scored on continuous metrics.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Counting cache lines: the traffic model and the padding bonus
md: Traffic ratio for a streaming loop is $S/k$: record size over bytes touched. For random access to whole records, the ratio flips against SoA by up to the number of fields.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Keep less: minimisation, retention schedules and legal holds
md: Deleting the primary copy is not deletion. Exports, tickets, caches, logs and backups each need their own retention, and backups usually expire last. Lesson 13 shows a way to make old backups unreadable all at once: encrypt them and destroy the key.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Where DLP acts: endpoints, email, web and cloud
md: Every exception is a hole. Allowlisting a whole team, a whole domain or a whole application because one rule was noisy removes protection from every future leak through that path. Fix the detector, then make narrow, reviewed exceptions with an expiry date.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: What Internet honeypots see: noise, bots and reused passwords
md: Internet-facing honeypots produce intelligence, internal decoys produce alerts. Never page someone for a hit on an Internet honeypot; feed its data into enrichment and blocklists instead.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Measuring value: the Tularosa study, metrics and practice
md: Judge deception by evidence: decoys placed on attack paths, tested regularly, alerts that reach a person fast and are mostly real, and at least one detection you would otherwise have missed.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Replaying failures, the limits of DST, and who uses it
md: DST turns rare, timing-dependent bugs into seeds. The engineering cost is up front (every source of nondeterminism behind an interface, plus good oracles), and the return is that every bug found is a bug you can replay and fix.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a secure pipeline, a response plan, practice
md: The question to ask of every part of a pipeline: who can change what this runs, and what can it reach when it does? If the answer to the first is "anyone who can open a PR" and to the second is "production", there is a gap, however many scanners run.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why parallel decoding breaks, and how to make it fast
md: Do not read 'parallel generation' as 'all tokens in one step'. Quality drops quickly when many interdependent tokens are committed together; useful systems unmask a few to a few dozen tokens per pass depending on confidence.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Moving the KV cache: bytes, links and overlap
md: Transfer cost = prompt tokens x bytes per token / bandwidth. Grouped-query attention, layer-wise streaming and placement on fast links make it small; slow links and long prompts at high rates make it the bottleneck.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: The registry in depth, and proving a USB drive was used
md: A VSN changes when a volume is reformatted and is only 32 bits on FAT, so a match is strong corroboration, not a unique fingerprint. Combine it with the device serial and times. The meanings of the 0x64 to 0x67 properties also vary by Windows build: test on a reference system before testifying to them.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: Vamana: RobustPrune and the alpha knob
md: A common misreading: larger alpha prunes *more*. It is the opposite. The removal test gets harder to pass as alpha grows, so more candidates survive, the average degree rises (up to the cap R), and search paths get shorter. The cost is memory and more distance computations per hop.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: KTO: aligning with thumbs up and thumbs down, no pairs
md: KTO keeps DPO's implicit reward and reference model but drops pairing: each example is scored against a shared reference point (the estimated KL drift) instead of against a sibling answer. That lets it train on binary feedback, and on imbalanced data via $\lambda_D, \lambda_U$.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Proving the new read path before trusting it
md: Scientist is for code that only reads. Its README says that because the candidate may or may not run, it is only safe for wrapping methods that do not change data. Write paths need different checks, such as comparing stored rows after the fact.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: The verifier: proving every path safe before it runs
md: The verifier runs once, at load time, and proves properties of **all** paths: bounded execution, typed pointers, null checks before dereference, initialized registers, in-bounds stack and map access. Because the proof is done up front, the JIT-compiled code needs no runtime checks and runs at native speed.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Edge devices: the doors attackers now try first
md: An edge appliance combines the three things attackers want most: anyone can talk to it before logging in, it holds credentials with reach inside, and it is usually the least observed computer you own.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Management interfaces: keep the admin door off the internet
md: The service may need the internet; the admin interface does not. Put management on its own network or behind a separate enforcement point, and prove it with an outside scan.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Why RL makes reasoning long: the length bias in the policy loss
md: Response length growth during RL is partly an optimizer artifact. Check the loss normalization (a constant normalizer as in Dr. GRPO, $\lambda < 1$ for PPO) and the mix of solvable problems before adding a length penalty, and log length separately for correct and incorrect rollouts.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Whether to think at all: NoThinking, hybrid modes and routing
md: The modes are far apart on hard problems. Qwen3-235B-A22B scored 85.7 on AIME 2024 thinking and 40.1 without. Fusion also had a price: for Qwen3-32B, thinking-mode AIME 2024 fell from 83.8 to 81.4 after the fusion and general-RL stages. A user-chosen switch is only as good as the user's guess about difficulty.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Unicode normalisation: NFC, NFD, NFKC and NFKD
md: UAX #15: "Normalization Forms KC and KD must not be blindly applied to arbitrary text", because they erase distinctions that can matter. Use NFKC (usually with case folding, next lesson) for identifiers such as usernames, and NFC for stored text you will show back to people.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: XML, multipart forms and email addresses: same bytes, different trees
md: For every structured format: one strict parser at the boundary, reject anything ambiguous (duplicate fields, malformed headers, unknown XML structure), and pass the parsed result, not the original bytes, to the rest of the system.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Process injection as telemetry: Sysmon events 8, 10 and 25
md: Misconception: "a GrantedAccess of 0x1FFFFF on LSASS is always an attack." Security products, backup agents and admin tools often request all access. Context decides: which signed program, how often, from which path, and with which call trace. Baseline the normal requesters on your hosts, then alert on the rest.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: One meter, many appliances: the disaggregation problem
md: NILM is an inverse problem: one observed sum, many hidden parts. Every algorithm you will meet differs only in what extra knowledge it uses to choose among the many decompositions that add up to the same total.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Blocking: compare only pairs that could match
md: A pair that blocking drops is classified as a non-match without ever being looked at. No scoring model can recover it. Use several strict rules joined by OR (Splink's advice: a longer list of strict rules beats a short list of loose ones), so a typo in one field is caught by a rule on another.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Who runs the tenant: Entra roles, Global Administrator and PIM
md: A service principal can hold an Entra admin role, and Microsoft names those that do as control plane assets. An app with Global Administrator, or with permission to assign roles, is a Global Administrator that has no MFA prompt to bypass. Review apps in role assignments with the same care as people.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Entra tokens: lifetimes, refresh tokens and revocation
md: Misconception: resetting a compromised user's password ends the attacker's access immediately. It revokes only refresh tokens obtained with the password (revoke sessions for the rest), and an access token already issued keeps working until it expires (up to 90 minutes) at any service that does not support CAE, and app sessions with their own cookies (the federation course's offboarding gap) are untouched.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Conditional Access in Entra: baselines and the gaps attackers use
md: Misconception: 'We have Conditional Access requiring MFA, so password spraying is solved.' Only for accounts and flows the policies cover. Excluded service accounts, legacy protocols if not blocked, and service principals with secrets all sit outside it, and attackers spray exactly those.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: A hardening baseline, an incident runbook, and where to practise
md: Baseline: few cloud-only admins on passkeys through PIM, restricted consent and reviewed apps, legacy auth and device code blocked, device-bound tokens where possible, hybrid bridges as Tier 0, and every log exported. Runbook: contain identities, hunt persistence in apps, devices and federation, scope data, evict at the root.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: The winner's curse: why the best public score is too high
md: Misconception: "we never trained on the test queries, so the number is clean." Choosing among variants by their test score is training with a very small model: one decision per comparison. A hundred prompt tweaks checked against the same 50 queries is a hundred-way fit.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: From bug to control: why exploit mitigations exist
md: A mitigation does not remove the bug. It removes one *route* from the bug to control. Patch the bug, prefer memory-safe languages for new code, and treat mitigations as the layer that protects you from the bugs you have not found yet.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Four independent counters that refuse to scale
md: The unit of sharing between cores is the cache line, not the variable. Two variables in one line are shared as far as the hardware is concerned, whatever the source code says.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: FedAvg exactly, worked on three clients over two rounds
md: With $E = 1$, full batches and full participation, FedAvg is exactly full-batch gradient descent on the pooled objective. Everything interesting about federated optimization, good and bad, comes from doing more than one local step.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Build it: a non-IID federated run in Flower, end to end
md: The one thing to remember: federated learning is an optimization algorithm shaped by a systems constraint. Every piece (averaging instead of gradient sharing, a quorum instead of a barrier, masks instead of raw updates, noise instead of trust) exists because rounds are expensive, clients are unreliable, and the server is not allowed to look.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Putting it together: routing in DeepSeek-V3
md: Batch-level balance has two weak spots the report names: imbalance inside a single sequence or small batch, and **domain shift** at inference (a deployment flooded with one kind of input overloads that domain's experts). V3 answers the first with large training batches plus the tiny sequence-wise loss, and the second with redundant experts at serving time.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Revocation is hard: dbx space, SBAT and secure version numbers
md: Every anti-rollback step also breaks old *legitimate* media. KB5025885 warns that enabling the PCA 2011 revocation on a device with the April 2026 or later updates sets SVN 5.0 in firmware, which invalidates older external boot media. Rebuild recovery media before you raise the floor.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: Online softmax: exact attention one block at a time
md: Online softmax is exact. The running max is only for numerical safety (keeping $e^x$ from overflowing); any consistent reference point gives the same $O/l$. Every FlashAttention version computes the same math; they differ only in how the work is mapped onto the hardware.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Tile sizes, GQA head fusion and JIT attention variants
md: FlashInfer = one block-sparse view of every KV layout, attention states merged exactly so work can be split and composed freely, a per-step plan that balances skewed lengths while staying CUDA-graph friendly, and a JIT template so new variants get fused kernels instead of new libraries.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Inductive invariants: from bounded checks to every N
md: An invariant is true in reachable states; an inductive invariant is preserved from *any* state that satisfies it. Model checking finds the first; proofs need the second. Use TLC or Apalache to debug a candidate before you try to prove it. Verus loop invariants, later in the course, carry the same three obligations.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Connecting specs to running code, and the wider tool map
md: Trace validation is testing, not proof: it checks only the runs you logged, and its verdict depends on choosing the right points in the code to log each atomic step. The paper says plainly that it does not provide formal correctness guarantees. Its strength is that it keeps a spec honest at the cost of logging.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Microscaling: one power-of-two scale per 32 values
md: MX formats move fine-grained scaling into hardware: 32 elements share one power-of-two E8M0 scale, applied by the tensor core during the dot product. For 8-bit elements that works well. For 4-bit elements the power-of-two restriction can waste up to a whole binade of FP4's tiny 3.58-binade range.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Scraping and enumeration: Facebook's 530 million phone numbers
md: Any feature that answers "is this identifier on the service, and whose is it" is an enumeration oracle. Cap it, gate it on consent, minimise its answer and watch its traffic.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Fake accounts and Sybil attacks
md: You cannot prove two accounts are two people (Douceur). Make each identity cost something scarce, give new accounts limited power until they earn trust, and look for accounts that act as a group.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Chargebacks, disputes and the true cost of a fraudulent order
md: Chargebacks are the fraud label, and they arrive weeks to months late. A fraudulent order costs goods, shipping and fees, several good orders' worth of margin.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Privacy and fairness of risk models
md: Collect what measurably helps, keep it only as long as needed, and keep it out of other uses. Then measure who your false positives are: an acceptable average can hide an unacceptable burden on one group.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: What vulnerability research is, and the rules you work under
md: Vulnerability research is a loop of find, triage, root-cause, report, fix. Its output is a fixed bug and a regression test, not an exploit, and it starts with permission.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Continuous fuzzing at scale: OSS-Fuzz, ClusterFuzz and Heartbleed
md: Continuous fuzzing turns fuzzing from an event into a property of the project: every commit is fuzzed, every crash is triaged, and fixed reproducers keep guarding the code. If your project parses untrusted input, it belongs in OSS-Fuzz or in ClusterFuzzLite (a lightweight version of ClusterFuzz that runs fuzzers in your CI pipeline).

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Writing the report and coordinating disclosure
md: Report privately with a minimised reproducer, the sanitizer output, a one-sentence root cause and a suggested fix; agree a disclosure date; publish an advisory with versions and credit once users can patch.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Geometric hashing: basis pairs, a hash table, and votes
md: A hard bin boundary is fragile: noise of a few thousandths can push u from 0.249 to 0.251 and the vote goes to the wrong bin. Practical systems search neighboring bins, or, like Astrometry.net, skip fixed bins and do a radius search in continuous code space.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Distance on a sphere, and why degree boxes break
md: Use great-circle distance for the final answer. The sphere itself is a model: the Earth is slightly flattened, and a spherical model gives errors typically up to 0.3%. That is why PostGIS `geography` defaults to `use_spheroid = true`, and Elasticsearch `geo_distance` defaults to `distance_type: arc` (the faster `plane` is documented as inaccurate over long distances and near the poles).

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Batching: why 32 launches lose to one
md: The per-image resize kernel does 0.44 microseconds of memory work and carries 0.9 to 6.7 microseconds of launch overhead. The GPU is idle or draining for most of the wall clock, and no kernel tuning can recover it. The fix is one launch that covers the whole batch.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Expandable segments: growing one segment with virtual memory
md: Fixed segments freeze their size at cudaMalloc time, so shapes that drift leave slivers. Expandable segments separate virtual addresses from physical memory (reserve once, map chunks as needed), so the segment grows contiguously instead.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Shared memory banks and bank conflicts
md: Bank = word index mod 32. Different words in one bank serialize; the same word broadcasts. For column access to a 2D tile, make the row width odd.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: The SOL gap: ranking many kernels by what they can return
md: SOL percentages are not the score you optimize. The triage guide is blunt about it: validate every change against absolute kernel duration, because SOL percentages can drop while the kernel gets faster, for example when you reduce the total work. Duration is the ground truth, not SOL percent.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Why chunk retrieval cannot answer 'what are the main themes?'
md: GraphRAG moves work from query time to indexing time. It pays many LLM calls up front to turn the corpus into a graph and a set of pre-written community summaries, so that global questions can be answered by reading summaries instead of sampling chunks.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Lighter graph RAG: FastGraphRAG, LightRAG, HippoRAG
md: Failure modes to watch in any LLM-built graph: missed entities in large chunks, duplicate nodes from name variants, hallucinated relationships stated with confidence, and summaries that drop the specific quotes users need. Every later stage inherits these errors, and global answers rarely show the raw evidence.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: DeepSeek-R1-Zero and R1: RLVR with GRPO at scale
md: "The model discovered reasoning on its own" is an overstatement. Liu et al. (2025, the Dr. GRPO paper you will meet in lesson 7) found that DeepSeek-V3-Base already shows aha-moment style self-reflection before any RL, and the R1 authors themselves say the vivid first-person reasoning style reflects engineered heuristics in the cold-start data. RL amplified behaviors already present in the base model.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Why old attacks still matter: five eras, five patterns
md: Each incident in this course is told the same way: what happened, why it worked (which pattern), what it cost, and what changed. The changes are the useful part: they are the controls you will be asked to run and defend.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Code Red, Slammer and Blaster: worms faster than people
md: "We patch monthly" did not save anyone from Slammer: the patch was six months old. What matters is whether the patch is actually installed on every exposed system, and whether services that need not face the internet (SQL Server's port 1434, Windows RPC) are reachable at all.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: NotPetya: a wiper delivered as a software update
md: NotPetya combined three patterns: a trusted supplier's update, a known flaw left open (EternalBlue) and reusable administrator credentials. Patching stopped only one of them. Unique credentials, segmentation and offline backups, including of the identity system, decided who recovered.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: perf record: sampling on overflow, and the skid problem
md: Without precise sampling, the "hot" instruction in `perf annotate` is often the one *after* the slow one, such as the instruction that consumes a load's result. Use `:pp` when you care about individual instructions.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Hardware supply chain, coordinated disclosure, and practice
md: Hardware security in one sentence: the hardware runs your program correctly, but not invisibly. Keep secrets out of shared state (constant-time code, isolation, separate secure processors), keep firmware and microcode current, measure what booted, and expect new variants.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: CL.0 and client-side desync: when a server ignores the body
md: Every code path must leave the connection in a known state: either it consumed exactly the declared body, or it closes the connection. Cache hits, redirects, errors and static files are the paths that forget.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: What 4 KiB pages cost a 16 GiB working set
md: Huge pages pay off three ways: one TLB entry covers 512 (or 262,144) times more memory, each miss walks fewer levels, and the page tables shrink. The kernel's THP doc calls the fourth effect, one page fault per 2 MiB instead of 512, almost irrelevant because it only happens on first touch.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Why a fixed-size state forgets and a KV cache does not
md: Pure SSMs are not simply worse. In the same NVIDIA study, Mamba-2 trained on 3.5T tokens beat the matching Transformer on average across standard zero-shot tasks. The gap is specific: copying, in-context learning and exact retrieval from the prompt.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion: fusing by rank, not score
md: RRF is not parameter-free. Bruch, Gai and Ingber (TOIS 2023, ACM Transactions on Information Systems) gave each retriever its own k and showed that nDCG swings noticeably when those constants are changed, and that constants tuned in-domain did not transfer reliably out of domain. Also, the window size is a hidden parameter: a document at rank 11 with a window of 10 contributes nothing at all.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: How a PLC thinks: the scan cycle and ladder logic
md: Changing a setpoint and changing the program are different. Setpoints are data the program reads (often over the network, by design, from the HMI). The program is the logic itself. Both can steer the process; defenders must watch and protect both.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Case: Ukraine 2015 and Industroyer 2016
md: It is tempting to read 2015 as 'malware turned off the lights'. Investigators found BlackEnergy but could not show it played a role in the outage; people turned off the lights, through legitimate remote access. Monitoring that only looks for malware would have missed it.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: One login, many apps: identity providers, service providers and trust
md: Misconception: SSO means one session. It means one *login*. After it, the IdP has a session and every app has its own, with its own cookie and lifetime. Disabling a user at the IdP does not end the app sessions already issued (lesson 10).

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Sessions across apps: IdP session, app sessions and logout
md: Offboarding gap: disabling a user at the IdP stops new logins, not existing app sessions or refresh tokens. A complete offboarding or account-takeover response also ends sessions in each app: through back-channel logout or signals where supported, through the app's admin API or SCIM deactivation (next lesson) where not.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Who has access, why, and who said so: identity governance
md: A common misconception is that identity and access management means single sign-on. Single sign-on proves who is logging in, once. It says nothing about whether Ana should still hold payroll access three jobs later. Governance works on the access itself, over time.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Just-in-time admin and break-glass accounts
md: A break-glass account that nobody monitors is just a permanent, policy-exempt Global Administrator. Its safety comes entirely from being rare, strongly authenticated, loudly alerted and regularly tested.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Cleaning the mask and correcting for lighting
md: Opening deletes every structure that cannot contain the kernel. A real change that is 1 or 2 pixels wide (a crack, a wire, a thin new road at low resolution) is erased along with the noise. Size the kernel from the smallest change you need to keep.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Evidence first: the order of volatility (RFC 3227)
md: RFC 3227 names programs to avoid on a live suspect system, such as `tar` or `xcopy`, because they update the access time of every file they touch, overwriting evidence of what the attacker read.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Communication: staff, customers, regulators and the legal clocks
md: Clocks start at awareness or determination, not at the end of the investigation. If you wait until you know everything, you will be late. Plan for phased notices: first what you know, then updates.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: MOVEit 2023: one SQL injection, thousands of victims
md: Patching closes the door but does not evict anyone already inside. After an injection that may have been exploited, look for persistence (web shells, new accounts, changed configuration) and for what data left, using web, database and network logs.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Fixed resources, polling, multishot networking and tradeoffs
md: io_uring turns I/O into **messages in shared memory**: batch them to amortize system calls, register files and buffers to cut per-request work, and use polling modes only where a spare CPU is worth the latency. The price is that correctness (lifetimes, ordering, CQ space) moves into your code.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Signed updates and anti-rollback: what a device must check
md: Fuses are a scarce, permanent budget. Bump the rollback version only when an old image has a security bug worth blocking, as MCUboot's separate security counter allows. Burn the bit only after the new image has proved it works (lesson 10), or a bad update could leave the device unable to boot anything.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Gadgets: from a polluted prototype to code execution (Kibana)
md: Do not read the hardening as "pollution is solved". It closes gadgets inside Node.js's own child_process code only. Your framework, template engine, HTTP client and your own options objects are full of optional properties, and every one is a possible gadget. The fix is still to stop pollution at the source.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Electron: when XSS in a desktop app becomes code execution
md: In Electron, every XSS is a candidate for code execution on the user's machine. The defaults (nodeIntegration off, contextIsolation on, sandbox on) are what keep XSS confined to the page; an app that turns any of them off, or runs an old Electron, has removed a wall. Lesson 16 covers the remaining walls you build yourself.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Histories: invoke, ok, fail, and the indeterminate info
md: Misconception: "a timeout means the request failed." A timeout means *you stopped waiting*. Writes, compare-and-sets and transaction commits that time out must be recorded as `:info` unless the error proves nothing was applied (for example, the request was rejected before it was sent).

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Measuring, caching and promoting without regressions
md: The most common autotuning self-deception is a "win" smaller than the confidence interval of the comparison. Report the interval, not just the ratio, and treat an interval that straddles 1.0 as "no difference found", not as a win.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The price of bypass, and when to choose something else
md: Bypass trades generality for cycles. It wins when per-operation overhead is the bottleneck and you can dedicate cores and devices; it loses when you need the kernel's protocols, tools, filesystems, isolation or power savings.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: The vulnerable driver blocklist: what it holds and how to deploy it
md: The blocklist uses **Authenticode** hashes, which skip the signature and checksum fields of the file. Sysmon, most EDRs and threat-intel feeds use **flat file** hashes (SHA-256 of every byte). The two do not match for the same signed driver. Build each list with the hash type its consumer computes.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Counting bytes: the chain before and after fusion
md: Fused bytes = what you must read + what you must keep. Everything in between is the saving. For a chain of k unary elementwise ops on the same tensor with no side outputs, eager moves about k times the fused bytes.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: A patient and consistent teacher: the recipe that makes KD work
md: Treat distillation as function matching: same input to teacher and student every step, as many distinct inputs as you can generate, and a schedule far longer than supervised training. Judge the run against a same-size model trained on labels, and track agreement with the teacher.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sizing the KV cache of Llama 3 8B, and why it caps batch size
md: KV bytes scale with layers x KV heads x head size x bytes per value x tokens x batch. Weights are paid once; the cache is paid per token per request, so at long context and large batch it dominates.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Keeping fewer tokens: windows, attention sinks and heavy hitters
md: Eviction scores are not free under fused attention. A method that needs every step's attention weights (H2O) needs eager attention, a second pass or a custom kernel. A method that scores once after prefill (SnapKV) leaves the decode kernel unchanged. With GQA, combine the scores over each group before choosing.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Build and test it: quantize real keys, then evict on a needle test
md: Question-aware compression works when the scoring queries are the question. Question-agnostic compression has to guess, and eviction cannot undo a wrong guess. Measure accuracy by needle depth, not only on average.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Eviction and placement: what stays, what sinks, what is dropped
md: Choose eviction by reuse pattern, not habit. LRU is a fine default; workloads with known future reuse (queued multi-turn sessions, scheduled agent steps) do much better with placement driven by the scheduler.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Why one vector per document leaves accuracy behind
md: Late interaction = independent encoding (so documents are precomputed) + token-level matching at query time (so fine-grained evidence is not averaged away into one vector).

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: The continuous thought: hidden state in, hidden state out
md: Misconception: a continuous thought is not the embedding of the most likely next word. It is never rounded to any vocabulary entry. Decoding it with the LM head is a diagnostic only.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Pause tokens, filler dots, recurrent depth and Coconut's costs
md: Loss of auditability is a design cost, not a detail. Latent thoughts can be probed with the LM head, but there is no readable trace to check. Pfau et al. raise the same concern: hidden computation can drift away from anything a human, or a behavior-based safety check, can read.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Error windows, exponential search and monotonic models
md: Bounded search costs the leaf's worst-case error on every lookup. Exponential search costs the error of this lookup. Tight models favour bounded search; loose models with mostly good predictions favour exponential search.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: Pointwise, pairwise and listwise approaches
md: A common mix-up: these families describe the **training loss**, not the model. A listwise-trained model still scores each document independently at serving time, so serving cost is the same for all three.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The state is a key-value memory, and it fills up
md: Bigger is not a free fix. Raising $d_k$ raises capacity, but state size and per-token compute grow as $d_k d_v$. The research direction instead is a smarter write rule, which is the next lesson.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Users, groups and root: /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow
md: Setting a user's shell to `/usr/sbin/nologin` or putting `*` in their password field does not fully disable them. The passwd manual notes such users may still run jobs through cron or log in by other means, and an SSH key in their home directory still works if the shell allows it. To retire an account, lock it, expire it and remove its keys.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: SSH: keys versus passwords, authorized_keys and hardening
md: Keys beat passwords because nothing guessable or reusable travels to the server. That moves the risk to the key files themselves: `authorized_keys` decides who gets in, so audit it like you audit sudoers.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: CIS Benchmarks: what one recommendation contains
md: CIS Benchmarks are consensus-written, product-specific configuration baselines with Level 1, Level 2 and STIG profiles. Each recommendation has a rationale, an audit check and a remediation, and maps to other frameworks, so one automated check can serve several auditors.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Writing audit rules that answer real questions
md: Write rules for questions, give every rule a key, use auid>=1000 together with auid!=unset, write b32 and b64 rules on x86-64, put never rules first, keep syscall rules few, and end production rule sets with -e 2.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Linux EDR and fleet telemetry: what sensors see and miss
md: Every sensor has a layer it watches and layers it cannot. Syscall hooks miss io_uring; host tools miss userland rootkits; nothing on the host reliably reports its own removal. Combine kernel-side sensors at LSM or kprobe level with off-host silence alerts.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a fleet plan, and where to practise
md: Inventory, patch, baseline, sandbox, watch, rebuild. Each is ordinary engineering on its own; run together as a loop on every host, they turn a fleet from 2,000 separate risks into one system you can measure.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: LLM judges for generation: modes, biases and fixes
md: A safe default for generation judging: pairwise or rubric grading with the explanation before the verdict; both orders, with disagreement treated as a tie; report and control length; a judge outside the model families being compared; and a human-labelled subset to measure agreement before every major change.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Continuous batching: scheduling every iteration
md: Continuous batching does **not** mean padding requests to a common length. The tokens are packed with no padding, and only attention looks at per-request boundaries. TensorRT-LLM's in-flight batching explicitly requires packed (unpadded) inputs for this reason.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: When the pool runs dry: admission control and preemption
md: Preemption is not free throughput. The optimistic policy's extra batch size is partly spent redoing prefills, and a preempted request's latency can jump by a full prefill plus queueing. Frequent preemption is a sign the pool is too small for the configured concurrency.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Why asking nicely for JSON is not enough
md: Three different promises are easy to confuse: *parses as JSON*, *matches my schema*, and *is correct*. JSON mode gives the first, schema-constrained output gives the second, and only your own validation and evaluation can check the third.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Evaluating the parser with exact match per field
md: The predictions in this lesson are hand-written to show typical error types. They are not measurements of any model. Use the method, not the numbers.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Prefix caching, truncation and smaller candidate lists
md: Every input saving has a quality price. Truncation can cut the sentence that made a passage relevant. A smaller $k$ means relevant documents retrieved at rank 31 or lower are never reranked. Measure NDCG@10 at each setting on your own queries before shipping the cheaper one.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Evaluating routers: cost-quality curves, PGR, APGR and CPT
md: Read router claims carefully. "2x cheaper at the same quality" depends on the benchmark, the model pair, the quality target and the baseline. RouteLLM's savings are measured against a random router, not against a GPT-4-only deployment, and vary from 1.41x to 3.66x across three benchmarks. Only an evaluation on your own prompts tells you what you will get.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: RANSAC: keeping only matches that agree on one homography
md: RANSAC finds the model that the most matches agree on by fitting minimal random samples. The cost grows as $1/w^s$, so cleaner matches (a good ratio test) and smaller samples make it dramatically cheaper.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Vyukov's bounded MPMC queue: a sequence number per cell
md: Vyukov is explicit: the queue is "not lockfree in the official meaning, just implemented by means of atomic RMW operations w/o mutexes" (RMW is read-modify-write: an instruction such as CAS or fetch-add that reads and writes a location in one indivisible step) and classifies it as having blocking producers and consumers. It is still excellent in practice; just do not cite it as a lock-free progress guarantee.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Drift when a release changes the format, and a pipeline that holds
md: The misconception that costs the most: that a template id is a stable name for a logging statement. It is a name for a *cluster*, and clusters split, merge, get wildcarded and get evicted. Anything long-lived (a dashboard, an alert rule, a trained model) must key on persisted template text plus an explicit supersedes relation, not on whatever integer the miner handed out last Tuesday.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: MITRE ATT&CK as a coverage map
md: A green cell is not protection. One rule tagged with a technique usually catches one or two of the many ways to perform it. Count a technique as covered only if a test of a realistic procedure produced an alert (lesson 17), and record which procedures were tested.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Position Interpolation and NTK-aware scaling
md: Do not confuse the two knobs. PI rescales *positions* (every pair by the same $1/s$). NTK-aware changes the *base* (each pair by a different amount). Both leave the model architecture unchanged; only the precomputed cos and sin tables differ.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Hiding communication, causal balance and Ulysses
md: Overlap condition: $c \ge F/B$. Fast links (NVLink, the TPU inter-chip interconnect or ICI) need blocks of about 1K tokens; slow links need tens of thousands. Causal masks require striping or zigzag chunk assignment, or the busiest rank sets the pace.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: What a loop can compute: algorithms, latent thoughts, fixed points
md: A loop is an algorithm's inner step. With enough iterations, a fixed-size block can resolve chains of references, simulate a small computer, or stand in for chain-of-thought steps, without adding parameters. How well *training* finds such a step is a separate, empirical question.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Learned depth per token: Mixture-of-Recursions, Ouro, HRM and TRM
md: Do not compare TRM's ARC numbers with LLM results as if they were the same kind of system. TRM is trained per task family on about 1000 augmented examples with a fixed answer grid; an LLM is a general text model. An independent ARC Prize analysis cited by the TRM paper found deep supervision drove most of HRM's gain (19% to 39%), while the two-level recursion added little (35.7% to 39.0%).

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: The wider PEFT family, and when LoRA falls short
md: Hu et al.'s footnote already warned that a small rank should not be expected to work for every task: if the target were a different language than pretraining, full fine-tuning (like LoRA with r equal to the model width) could win. Low intrinsic rank was measured on tasks that are close to what the model already knows.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Unlearning by replacement: Who's Harry Potter and RMU
md: Near-chance accuracy on a multiple-choice proxy shows the model no longer *answers* those questions. It does not show the knowledge is gone from the weights. The WMDP authors say so themselves: because RMU edits only three layers it "perhaps obfuscates knowledge more than unlearns it", and in their appendix fine-tuning on the forget corpus recovered the performance.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: How a Mac defends itself: the layers from boot to app
md: "Macs don't get viruses" is a myth defenders still meet. Information stealers such as Atomic Stealer (lesson 16) have been sold to criminals as a monthly service since 2023, and Microsoft documented new campaigns delivering them to Macs in 2026. The built-in controls are strong, but they mostly decide what may *launch*; social engineering goes around them.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Unified logging: reading what the Mac recorded
md: Do not expect an attacker's password prompt, curl URL or file path to show up in plain text in the unified log. Default privacy redaction hides many dynamic strings. Plan on Endpoint Security or EDR telemetry for process command lines, and use the unified log for subsystem state changes.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: What malware is, and the families analysts name
md: NIST notes that most samples blend several categories, so the classic labels are 'considerably less useful than they used to be' for incident handling. Use the labels to communicate quickly; spend your time on behaviour and detection.
